title: Ironbank Fintech — Procurement + DPA redlines (Redwood Dedicated/Private)
summary: Procurement/legal review focused on Ironbank redlines to Redwood’s DPA for a Dedicated (and possible Private/VPC) deployment. Key points: data retention defaults and controls (request/response logs, prompt/output storage), deletion timelines, subprocessor notice, audit language, SCCs/UK addendum, breach notification window, and liability alignment with MSA. Ironbank wants written confirmation that Redwood does not use customer content for training and that log retention can be reduced/disabled for regulated workloads. Target signature discussed for end of June, pending DPA markup turnaround and security evidence package.
topics: DPA redlines; Data retention and log controls; SOC 2 evidence + audit rights; Subprocessors + notice period; SCCs / UK IDTA addendum; Breach notification SLA; Timeline to signature; Dedicated vs Private/VPC packaging
action_items: Michael Grant (Redwood Legal) — Return DPA redlines with proposed compromise language (audit clause, subprocessor notice, liability tie-in) — due 2025-06-06
Dr. Aisha Rahman (Redwood Security) — Send evidence package (SOC 2 report excerpt/bridge letter, encryption-at-rest/in-transit statement, retention controls doc, subprocessor list) — due 2025-06-05
Tom Nguyen (Ironbank Procurement) — Confirm whether Ironbank requires UK addendum in addition to SCCs and provide preferred template — due 2025-06-04
Elena Morozova (Ironbank Eng) — Provide required retention settings (0/7/14/30 days) for prompts/outputs and operational logs for production — due 2025-06-07
next_steps: Redwood to send redlined DPA response + clean copy options (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) by Friday.
Ironbank to confirm retention requirements and whether VPC/Private is mandatory for production.
Schedule 30-min follow-up for final DPA walkthrough early next week; hold signature target for week of June 24.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai transcription

Date: 2025-06-03
Time: 2:00pm ET
Duration: 47 min
Call type: Procurement / legal process

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering), Michael Grant (Legal), Dr. Aisha Rahman (Security)
Ironbank Fintech: Tom Nguyen (Procurement), Samantha Lee (Legal), Raj Patel (Security/Risk), Elena Morozova (Eng)

---

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is basically: walk through the DPA markups and unblock the last couple items so we can keep the end-of-month target.

[00:14] Tom Nguyen: Yep, thanks Avery. This is kind of the last big gate on our side, besides pricing finalization, but legal wants the language settled before we queue signature.

[00:24] Samantha Lee: Hi. I sent over the redline version yesterday. It’s mostly standard but we do have a few non-negotiables because of our regulatory posture.

[00:34] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Michael and Aisha are on as well. Michael can handle the legal text; Aisha can confirm the security and retention controls.

[00:43] Markus Klein: And I can jump in if we need to get specific on what is stored where in the product.

[00:48] Samantha Lee: Great.

[01:02] Fireflies (auto): Meeting summary will be generated after the call.

[01:06] Avery Johnson: Samantha, do you want to start with the top items?

[01:10] Samantha Lee: Sure. First one is data retention and deletion. In your DPA, Section 4 says you may retain “Customer Data” as necessary for security and debugging, but it doesn’t define a maximum period or give us the right to set it to zero.

[01:26] Samantha Lee: For our workload, prompts and outputs can include personal data. We need a clear retention period, and ideally the ability to configure it, and deletion within, we said 30 days.

[01:38] Markus Klein: Yep, makes sense. So operationally, there are two buckets: content logs (request/response payloads) and platform logs (metadata like timestamps, token counts, error codes). For Dedicated we can disable payload logging, or set it to a short window. Platform logs we keep longer for SRE and billing reconciliation.

[01:58] Raj Patel: When you say “disable payload logging,” does that mean you do not store the prompt/response at all? Or it’s just not visible in the console?

[02:07] Markus Klein: It means we do not persist the raw prompt/response body to our logging store. There can still be transient data in memory for processing the request, obviously.

[02:18] Raj Patel: Okay. We need that written, not just “we can.”

[02:22] Dr. Aisha Rahman: That’s fair. We can provide a control statement: “Customer content is not retained beyond transient processing unless logging is enabled.” For Dedicated/Private, default is minimal and configurable.

[02:35] Samantha Lee: Also, your deletion clause references “within a reasonable time.” We need a defined SLA and alignment to deletion requests.

[02:43] Michael Grant: Understood. We typically commit to 30 days for deletion from active systems, and longer for backups where applicable, but we can be more precise. Some customers request 14 days. There’s also the nuance that billing records can’t be retroactively deleted in some jurisdictions; but those records should not include content, only usage.

[03:06] Elena Morozova: Just to anchor, our intended production is card-adjacent workflows. We’re trying to avoid any storage of content. Usage metrics are fine.

[03:15] Avery Johnson: And from the commercial side, we’ve been talking about Dedicated as the starting point, with an option to go Private/VPC if required by your internal policy. So we want the DPA to support either.

[03:28] Tom Nguyen: Right now risk is leaning VPC. But we’re not sure if that’s a hard requirement yet. That’s why the retention settings are key.

[03:38] Samantha Lee: Second item: “training.” We need the DPA to clearly say you will not use our data to train models, period.

[03:46] Avery Johnson: Yeah, that’s consistent with what we’ve said. We do not train on customer content.

[03:51] Michael Grant: The DPA as drafted says we only process on instructions and do not use for advertising or training. Your redline changes that to a stronger prohibition. I think we can accept that, but we may need to preserve an exception for aggregated, de-identified telemetry for service improvement. Not content. Telemetry.

[04:12] Raj Patel: Telemetry is fine if it’s truly de-identified. But we want it clearly defined.

[04:18] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We can specify that telemetry excludes prompt/response content, includes things like token counts, latency, error types, and maybe model ID, region.

[04:28] Samantha Lee: Great.

[04:33] Samantha Lee: Third, subprocessors. You have a 30-day notice period. We asked for 60 days and the ability to object.

[04:42] Michael Grant: We can do 30, and we do allow objection with commercially reasonable alternatives. 60 is difficult because we sometimes need to add vendors quickly for reliability. But for regulated customers we can discuss a “material change” notice. Let me propose language: 30 days for planned changes, and as soon as reasonably practicable for emergency changes.

[05:05] Tom Nguyen: What’s your current subprocessor list? We need it on file.

[05:09] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We maintain an up-to-date subprocessor page. For Dedicated, it’s primarily cloud infrastructure providers and monitoring. For Private, it can be fewer depending on deployment. I’ll send the list with the evidence package.

[05:23] Samantha Lee: Okay. Fourth: audit rights. We inserted on-site audit rights and annual audit.

[05:31] Michael Grant: This is the one we need to narrow. We can’t support on-site audits for each customer in practice. We provide SOC 2 Type II report, we can support reasonable questionnaires, and we can support a right to audit via a third-party report.

[05:49] Raj Patel: Our policy says “right to audit” must exist, but it can be satisfied by SOC 2 if it’s scoped appropriately. We need that explicitly.

[05:59] Michael Grant: Great. We can revise to say: audits are satisfied by providing SOC 2 report and supporting additional information requests; on-site audit only if (a) required by law or regulator, and (b) subject to mutual agreement.

[06:17] Samantha Lee: That’s likely acceptable.

[06:21] Avery Johnson: If helpful, we’ve done that exact compromise with other fintechs.

[06:27] Samantha Lee: Fifth: cross-border transfers. We need SCCs and UK addendum.

[06:34] Michael Grant: We already incorporate SCCs by reference for EU data transfers. For the UK, we can attach the UK addendum. Question: do you need IDTA specifically, or UK addendum to SCCs? Different counsel prefer one.

[06:49] Samantha Lee: We need UK addendum. I’ll confirm with our outside counsel but that’s standard.

[06:56] Tom Nguyen: Also do you have data residency options? Like if we require EU-only later.

[07:03] Markus Klein: For Hosted, we have regions; for Dedicated, we can allocate capacity in a specific region. For Private/VPC, it’s within your cloud account / VPC boundary, depending on architecture. But yes, you can do EMEA-only.

[07:20] Raj Patel: If we do Dedicated in US region, does data ever leave that region? Like support access?

[07:27] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Support access is controlled. Access to systems is logged, and we can restrict support to metadata only. If payload logging is disabled, there’s no content to access. Cross-region replication depends on your configuration; for Dedicated we can keep logs regional.

[07:46] Elena Morozova: Sorry, can I ask a product question? In the evaluation we did last month, we were on the Hosted API with a trial key. Are the retention controls different there?

[07:56] Markus Klein: Yes. Hosted is more standardized. Dedicated/Private give you stronger controls. That’s one reason the PLG-to-sales signal triggered this motion: you hit a spend velocity threshold and then you were looking at security docs and Dedicated docs, so we proactively suggested the upgrade.

[08:16] Avery Johnson: Yeah, and then you opened the procurement track.

[08:19] Tom Nguyen: That makes sense. We’re fine that it started PLG, but we need contract posture now.

[08:27] Samantha Lee: Sixth: breach notification. You have “without undue delay.” We need a 72-hour window.

[08:35] Michael Grant: We can commit to 72 hours from confirmation of a breach involving your personal data. We’ll want to clarify it’s from confirmation, not suspicion, to avoid noise.

[08:48] Raj Patel: That’s standard.

[08:52] Samantha Lee: Seventh: liability. Our redline ties DPA liability to the MSA cap and excludes carve-outs.

[09:02] Michael Grant: Right now our DPA aligns to the MSA. We can keep it that way. If your MSA asks for super-cap for data incidents, that’s a commercial discussion. But the DPA itself usually references the MSA limits.

[09:17] Tom Nguyen: We’re not trying to get a super-cap right now. We just want it to be consistent.

[09:22] Avery Johnson: Great.

[09:26] Fireflies (auto): Topics detected: DPA redlines, retention, audit, SCC, breach notification.

[09:32] Samantha Lee: Now, retention specifics. Markus, you said two buckets. We need the DPA to distinguish them. Right now “Customer Data” is too broad.

[09:41] Markus Klein: Agreed. The product view: content data (prompts, completions, embeddings vectors) is “customer content.” Operational metadata is “usage telemetry.” We can define those terms.

[09:53] Raj Patel: Do you store embeddings vectors? That’s content-adjacent.

[09:58] Markus Klein: In the Hosted API, we process and return vectors; we do not store them by default. Customers might store them in their own vector DB. In some debugging cases, if payload logging is enabled, it could capture the request. But again, that’s controllable.

[10:15] Elena Morozova: For our use case, we’re generating embeddings and then storing them ourselves. We don’t want Redwood to store any.

[10:22] Dr. Aisha Rahman: That aligns. We can provide an attestation-style statement: “By default, Redwood does not persist customer embeddings/prompt content; optional logging is configurable and can be disabled.”

[10:37] Samantha Lee: Okay. Another nuance: backups. You mentioned backups might extend the deletion timeline.

[10:44] Michael Grant: Yes. Typical cloud backups can retain data for a set period. But if we are not storing content logs, backups shouldn’t include content. They could include config metadata. We can specify that deletion applies to active systems within 30 days and backups are overwritten on a rolling schedule, e.g., 35-90 days depending.

[11:06] Raj Patel: Our preference is a maximum of 35 days for backups.

[11:10] Dr. Aisha Rahman: For Dedicated/Private, we can align backup retention to your requirement; but it may affect recovery objectives. We should separate “customer content” vs “system configuration.”

[11:25] Elena Morozova: If Private is in our VPC, are backups in our control?

[11:29] Markus Klein: In true Private in your environment, yes. In “VPC-hosted by Redwood,” it’s in a dedicated VPC but managed by us; backups are managed but can be configured.

[11:44] Tom Nguyen: We’ll need to decide which model. But for the contract, we want the strictest wording possible.

[11:53] Avery Johnson: Right, though we need it to remain operationally accurate for the deployment you pick.

[11:59] Samantha Lee: Understood.

[12:02] Samantha Lee: Also: data location. Our redline says “all processing in the US.” But we may expand to UK.

[12:10] Michael Grant: We can specify “primary processing region as selected by Customer,” and we will not move content outside that region except on your instructions.

[12:24] Raj Patel: Great.

[12:27] Samantha Lee: Security measures exhibit: we asked for encryption, access controls, logging, and key management.

[12:35] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We can attach a security exhibit. High-level: TLS in transit; encryption at rest; role-based access; SSO/SAML for the console; audit logs for admin actions; and for Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS. Dedicated supports customer-managed keys in some configurations.

[12:58] Raj Patel: “Some configurations” is squishy. We need a yes/no.

[13:03] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Fair. For Private in your cloud account: yes, you use your KMS keys. For Dedicated that we operate: we can support CMEK in certain clouds, but it depends on the storage layer. If CMEK is mandatory, that’s an argument for Private.

[13:23] Avery Johnson: We can take that as an input to packaging. If CMEK is must-have, Private is probably the right fit.

[13:30] Tom Nguyen: That may increase cost.

[13:32] Avery Johnson: It does, but it also aligns to your policy. We can do a phased approach—Dedicated for the pilot, Private for production—if risk approves.

[13:43] Elena Morozova: I’d rather not re-platform midstream but okay.

[13:47] Markus Klein: It’s the same API surface. Operationally you switch endpoints and some network config. But yes, there’s a migration step.

[14:02] Samantha Lee: Another legal item: confidentiality. We added “prompt and output” explicitly.

[14:09] Michael Grant: We can accept that. Prompt and output are customer confidential information.

[14:16] Raj Patel: And access logging—do you provide logs of your staff access?

[14:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We log administrative access. For enterprise tiers, we can provide audit logs and, upon request, reports of access events. We don’t generally stream you our internal logs, but we can provide evidence.

[14:37] Raj Patel: Okay.

[14:40] Fireflies (auto): Action items detected.

[14:45] Avery Johnson: Samantha, are there any “must change today” items?

[14:50] Samantha Lee: The big ones: (1) no training, (2) retention defined and configurable, (3) audit rights satisfied by SOC 2, (4) SCC + UK addendum, (5) deletion SLA.

[15:04] Michael Grant: I think we can address all of those in our counter-redline.

[15:09] Tom Nguyen: What’s the turnaround? We’re trying to keep signature by end of June.

[15:14] Michael Grant: If you can accept the audit compromise and 30-day subprocessor notice with emergency exception, we can return by Friday.

[15:23] Samantha Lee: Friday is fine.

[15:26] Avery Johnson: Great. Then we can schedule a quick 30-minute call early next week to finalize.

[15:34] Elena Morozova: I also have a question on retention controls in the product UI. Is it a setting we can verify?

[15:40] Markus Klein: For Dedicated/Private, yes. It’s part of the deployment config—logging level, retention days. We can show it in the console or config file depending.

[15:53] Elena Morozova: Okay.

[15:55] Raj Patel: Can you confirm that you do not store API keys in plain text?

[15:59] Markus Klein: Correct. We store hashed/secured secrets; and for Private, you can manage keys through your secret manager.

[16:10] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And we support key rotation, and we can include that in the security exhibit.

[16:18] Samantha Lee: One more clause: data subject requests. We want you to assist within 10 business days.

[16:25] Michael Grant: We can commit to commercially reasonable assistance, but a hard 10 days can be tricky if the request is complex. We can do 15 business days, or “promptly and in any event within 30 days” consistent with GDPR timelines.

[16:41] Samantha Lee: Our internal is 10. But okay, let me see if “promptly” plus a max works.

[16:47] Raj Patel: For us, the risk is you having content at all. If content logging is off, DSAR is easier.

[16:55] Samantha Lee: True.

[17:00] Avery Johnson: Right, the technical control reduces the compliance surface.

[17:06] Tom Nguyen: Can we talk about timeline more concretely? If we get DPA done next week, when do we start production?

[17:13] Elena Morozova: We’re targeting July for a controlled rollout. Our eval already hit throughput targets on Hosted, but we need Dedicated numbers.

[17:22] Markus Klein: We can run the benchmark on Dedicated as soon as we have a signed order form and can provision capacity. Typically 1-2 weeks to provision, faster if we have inventory.

[17:36] Avery Johnson: And in parallel, we can work through security review. The PLG signal already kicked off the security doc requests, so we’re ahead.

[17:45] Raj Patel: We still need the SOC 2 report and the subprocessor list.

[17:49] Dr. Aisha Rahman: I’ll send by Thursday.

[17:52] Samantha Lee: About SOC 2: will you provide the full report or a bridge letter?

[17:57] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Under NDA, we can provide the full report. If you prefer, we can provide a bridge letter plus relevant sections.

[18:06] Raj Patel: Full report under NDA.

[18:08] Michael Grant: We can arrange that. We’ll ensure NDA is in place.

[18:12] Tom Nguyen: NDA is already executed.

[18:15] Avery Johnson: Great.

[18:18] Samantha Lee: Another redline: we added a clause about “no commingling” of data. For Dedicated that’s easy, for Hosted it’s not.

[18:28] Markus Klein: Right. Hosted is multi-tenant. Dedicated is isolated compute and data plane for your org. For Private it’s even more isolated.

[18:39] Michael Grant: We can scope that clause to Dedicated/Private and not Hosted. Otherwise it’s inaccurate.

[18:46] Samantha Lee: Okay.

[18:50] Raj Patel: Any third-party model providers in the loop? Like are you calling OpenAI behind the scenes?

[18:56] Markus Klein: No. Redwood runs the models on our infrastructure. We’re not proxying to OpenAI. You can choose open models from our catalog or bring a model. But it’s served on our runtime.

[19:10] Raj Patel: Good. We just wanted to avoid unknown subprocessors.

[19:15] Avery Johnson: That’s also why Dedicated helps—clear boundary.

[19:20] Samantha Lee: I think that covers the DPA. We have a separate MSA but not today.

[19:26] Michael Grant: Yep.

[19:28] Avery Johnson: Before we wrap, can we confirm the decision on UK addendum? Tom, can you confirm what you need?

[19:36] Tom Nguyen: I’ll confirm with counsel, but assume yes.

[19:39] Samantha Lee: Yes, we’ll want UK addendum.

[19:43] Michael Grant: Great.

[19:46] Avery Johnson: Raj, anything else from security side?

[19:49] Raj Patel: Retention controls doc is key. Also an answer to “can you set it to zero?” We’d like a yes for content logs.

[19:58] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes for content payload logs. For operational logs, not zero, but we can minimize. We’ll put this in writing.

[20:11] Raj Patel: Perfect.

[20:14] Elena Morozova: One more. If we do Dedicated, do you support customer-managed networking, like private link?

[20:22] Markus Klein: Yes, private connectivity options exist. Depending on cloud, PrivateLink / peering. For Private deployment it’s native. We can follow up separately.

[20:33] Avery Johnson: We’ll park that for the SE session. Today is DPA.

[20:37] Samantha Lee: Okay.

[20:40] Fireflies (auto): Question detected: Can retention be set to zero for content logs?

[20:44] Avery Johnson: Let’s recap next steps so we’re all aligned.

[20:48] Avery Johnson: One: Michael returns DPA counter-redline by Friday. Two: Aisha sends security evidence package by Thursday. Three: Tom confirms UK addendum template preference. Four: Elena sends retention requirement specifics.

[21:07] Tom Nguyen: Sounds right.

[21:09] Samantha Lee: Yes.

[21:11] Raj Patel: Good.

[21:12] Elena Morozova: Yep.

[21:14] Avery Johnson: Then we schedule a 30-minute finalization call early next week.

[21:19] Tom Nguyen: Please propose times.

[21:22] Avery Johnson: Will do.

[21:25] Markus Klein: And Elena, I’ll send you a short note on the retention knobs and what’s possible in Dedicated vs Private.

[21:32] Elena Morozova: Thanks.

[21:34] Avery Johnson: Anything else before we drop?

[21:37] Samantha Lee: No, thank you.

[21:40] Raj Patel: Thanks.

[21:41] Tom Nguyen: Thanks all.

[21:43] Avery Johnson: Great, talk soon.
